title: Molecular Evolution, Modelling and Computer-Based Drug Design
tagline: Trace how sequences evolve, predict how proteins fold and move, and use computers to find molecules that fit them.
overview: This course joins three connected fields: molecular evolution (substitution models, alignment, phylogenetics, selection and gene duplication), molecular modelling (homology modelling, AlphaFold and molecular dynamics) and computer-aided drug design (docking, virtual screening, QSAR, pharmacophores, ADMET and machine learning). Each unit includes a hands-on computational component, reflecting the 30 hours of lectures and 30 hours of practical work: BLAST and EMBOSS, Clustal Omega and IQ-TREE or MEGA, SWISS-MODEL and AlphaFold DB, GROMACS, AutoDock Vina, SwissADME and RDKit. The topics follow the standard content of the course title at BSc Honours level.
whyItMatters: Computational modelling now guides decisions in drug discovery, vaccine design, enzyme engineering and pathogen surveillance. Knowing how to build and critique a tree, a model or a docking experiment lets you evaluate claims in the literature and run credible in silico projects of your own.
studyTips: Do every practical twice: once following a tutorial, then again on your own protein or gene to prove you understand it.
Keep a lab notebook (or a Jupyter notebook) with exact commands, versions and parameters so results are reproducible.
For every result, ask what would make it wrong: a bad alignment, a wrong protonation state, a leaky test set.
Learn the basics of the command line and Python early; they pay off in every unit.

units.title: Foundations of Molecular Evolution
units.hook: When Zuckerkandl and Pauling compared haemoglobins from different species in the 1960s, they noticed that the number of amino acid differences grew roughly in step with the time since the species split. Proteins seemed to carry a faint ticking clock. Why they tick, and why the ticking is not always steady, is the foundation of everything else in this course.
learningObjectives: Explain how mutation, drift and selection together determine the fate of a new variant.
State the central claim of the neutral theory and how it differs from a purely selectionist view.
Explain the molecular clock hypothesis and list reasons it can be violated.
Describe nucleotide substitution models (JC69, K80, HKY85, GTR) and why we correct for multiple hits.
Distinguish synonymous from non-synonymous substitutions and say why they evolve at different rates.
Calculate a simple p-distance and a Jukes-Cantor corrected distance from an alignment.

keyConcepts.definition: A mutation that has spread through a population until it is fixed; the unit of long-term molecular evolution.
Random change in allele frequencies from sampling in finite populations; the dominant force for neutral variants.
Kimura's proposal that most fixed molecular differences between species are due to random drift of selectively neutral mutations, not positive selection.
Ohta's extension: slightly deleterious mutations behave as neutral in small populations but are removed by selection in large ones.
The hypothesis that substitutions accumulate at a roughly constant rate for a given gene, so genetic distance can be used to estimate divergence times.
Selection that removes deleterious variants and keeps functionally important sites conserved.
Several substitutions at the same site over time, so observed differences underestimate the true number of changes.
Transitions swap purine with purine or pyrimidine with pyrimidine (A-G, C-T) and occur more often than transversions.
A model in which substitution rates vary among lineages, estimated statistically while dating a tree.

deeper.beginner: Imagine copying a manuscript by hand over thousands of years. Most copying slips make no difference to the meaning, a few damage it and are removed, and very rarely one improves it. Counting the differences between two copies tells you roughly how long ago they separated, as long as the scribes copied at a steady speed. The analogy breaks because real evolutionary rates change with generation time, population size and selection.
deeper.intermediate: Under neutral evolution, the rate of substitution equals the neutral mutation rate, independent of population size. This gives the clock its logic, but generation time effects mean that rates per year differ between mice and humans. Synonymous sites generally evolve faster than non-synonymous sites because most amino acid changes are mildly harmful. Observed differences (p-distance) are corrected for unseen multiple hits with models; the Jukes-Cantor correction is d = -(3/4) ln(1 - 4p/3), and more realistic models add unequal base frequencies (HKY85), different transition and transversion rates, and gamma-distributed rate variation among sites.
deeper.advanced: Calibrating a molecular clock needs independent dates (fossils, geological events), and uncertainty in calibrations propagates into all dated nodes; Bayesian relaxed-clock methods (BEAST, MCMCTree) jointly estimate rates and times. Selection for protein function means that rates vary among sites; amino acid models (JTT, WAG, LG) and site-heterogeneous mixtures (CAT, C60) capture this. Practical (about 3 h): compute p-distance and corrected distance for a set of globin sequences in MEGA and compare them with the number of observed differences to see saturation.

commonMistakes: Believing neutral theory says selection is unimportant; it says most molecular differences are neutral, not that adaptation never happens.
Using raw p-distance for distantly related sequences; ignoring multiple hits underestimates divergence.
Assuming one clock rate applies to all genes and lineages.

units.title: Sequence Alignment and Database Searching (Practical)
units.hook: A single BLAST search can tell you that a protein you just sequenced from a Sri Lankan soil bacterium looks like an enzyme from a hot-spring microbe on another continent. That search is built on a dynamic-programming idea from 1970 and a heuristic that made it fast enough to run against every known sequence.
learningObjectives: Explain the logic of global (Needleman-Wunsch) and local (Smith-Waterman) alignment using dynamic programming.
Choose and interpret a substitution matrix (PAM, BLOSUM) and gap penalties.
Distinguish identity, similarity and homology.
Run BLASTn, BLASTp and tBLASTn and interpret bit score, E-value, query coverage and percent identity.
Explain how BLAST uses seeds to be fast and what it can miss (remote homologs, PSI-BLAST, profile HMMs).
Perform a pairwise alignment with EMBOSS Needle/Water and a Biopython script and compare outputs.

keyConcepts.definition: Aligns two sequences end to end; Needleman-Wunsch finds the optimal score by dynamic programming.
Finds the best-scoring segments within sequences; Smith-Waterman, the basis of searches for shared domains.
A table of log-odds scores for aligning each pair of residues; BLOSUM62 is the default for protein searches.
A cost for opening and extending a gap, usually affine (open plus extend), reflecting that indels are rarer than substitutions.
The number of alignments with score at least as good that are expected by chance in a database of that size; smaller means more significant.
A normalised alignment score independent of the scoring matrix, allowing comparison between searches.
Shared ancestry; an all-or-none statement. Percent identity is a measure of similarity, not of homology.
A short word match (for example 3 residues for proteins) with a threshold score, extended to a full alignment if it passes.
Iterated search using a position-specific scoring matrix or hidden Markov model to detect remote homologs.

deeper.beginner: To align two sequences you try every way of sliding them against each other and inserting gaps, scoring matches up and mismatches and gaps down, and keep the best. Dynamic programming does this without trying every combination by filling a grid. BLAST makes the process fast by first looking for short exact-ish words and extending only those.
deeper.intermediate: Substitution matrices reflect observed amino acid replacements in conserved blocks: BLOSUM62 is derived from blocks clustered at 62 percent identity and suits moderately divergent sequences. For a protein in the twilight zone (roughly 20-35 percent identity) a high identity can still be insignificant if the alignment is short, so always read E-value and coverage. Hands-on (about 4 h): run BLASTp for a protein of interest against Swiss-Prot and nr, record top hits, change the matrix and the word size, align two homologs with EMBOSS Needle (global) and Water (local), and compare.
deeper.advanced: E-values depend on the database size and statistical parameters (Karlin-Altschul), so the same alignment has a different E-value in a bigger database. Low-complexity regions are masked to avoid spurious hits. Remote homology detection improves with profile methods (PSI-BLAST, HMMER, HHblits) that use many sequences to capture position-specific conservation, and with structure-based searches such as Foldseek. In Biopython, PairwiseAligner reproduces the dynamic-programming matrices so students can verify hand calculations.

commonMistakes: Equating percent identity with homology: sequences are either homologous or not, while identity is graded.
Reading E-values without checking query coverage; a tiny, perfect match can have a low E-value but cover a small fraction of the query.
Using BLASTn for distant relationships; protein-level searches are far more sensitive for divergent genes.

units.title: Multiple Sequence Alignment and Phylogenetic Trees (Practical)
units.hook: A phylogenetic tree is a hypothesis about who is related to whom, and it is only as good as the alignment and model behind it. In a few hours you can take genes from a dozen species, align them and watch a tree appear, and then learn how to doubt it properly.
learningObjectives: Describe progressive multiple sequence alignment (Clustal Omega, MUSCLE, MAFFT) and when to trim alignments.
Read a phylogenetic tree: tips, nodes, branches, clades, root and outgroup.
Compare distance (UPGMA, neighbour-joining), parsimony, maximum likelihood and Bayesian methods.
Select a substitution model with ModelFinder or MEGA's model test and justify the choice.
Assess support using bootstrap and posterior probability and say what they do and do not mean.
Build, annotate and interpret a tree from raw sequences using Clustal Omega, IQ-TREE or MEGA and iTOL.

keyConcepts.definition: An alignment of three or more homologous sequences that places homologous residues in the same column.
A group consisting of an ancestor and all its descendants (monophyletic group).
A lineage known to have diverged earlier than the group of interest, used to root the tree.
A fast distance method that builds a tree by repeatedly joining the pair of nodes that minimises total tree length; produces an unrooted tree.
Chooses the tree needing the fewest evolutionary changes; can be misled by long branches.
Chooses the tree and parameters that make the observed alignment most probable under an explicit substitution model.
Estimates the posterior distribution of trees via MCMC, giving posterior probabilities for clades.
The percentage of resampled alignments in which a clade appears; a measure of how consistently the data support it.
An artefact in which fast-evolving lineages group together because of chance similarities, not shared ancestry.

deeper.beginner: A tree is built by aligning sequences column by column and asking what pattern of ancestry best explains the differences. Branch lengths tell you how much change has happened; where the branches join tells you the order of splitting. Rotating branches at a node does not change the tree, just as turning a mobile does not change which pieces are attached to which.
deeper.intermediate: Alignment errors propagate directly into the tree, so inspect and, where necessary, trim poorly aligned regions (trimAl, Gblocks). Maximum likelihood with a good model (selected by AIC or BIC) is the usual default; IQ-TREE adds ultrafast bootstrap, where support of 95 percent or more is considered fairly reliable. Hands-on (about 4 h): fetch orthologous sequences from UniProt, align with Clustal Omega, run model selection and ML in MEGA or IQ-TREE, and visualise and annotate in iTOL.
deeper.advanced: Support values are not probabilities of truth: bootstrap measures the stability of a result under resampling, and it can be high for a wrong tree if the model is badly misspecified. Gene trees differ from species trees because of incomplete lineage sorting, duplication, loss and horizontal transfer, and coalescent-based methods (ASTRAL) or concatenation with partitioned models are used for species-level trees. Dating a tree requires a clock model and calibrations, as in BEAST.

commonMistakes: Reading species relationships from the order of tips; only the branching pattern matters.
Treating a gene tree as the species tree.
Using an alignment of non-homologous or poorly aligned regions and trusting the tree anyway.

units.title: Detecting Selection, Gene Duplication and Horizontal Transfer (Practical)
units.hook: Some amino acid positions in a viral surface protein change so quickly that they leave a statistical fingerprint of an arms race. Others, like the active site of a metabolic enzyme, barely change over billions of years. Reading those fingerprints, and tracing how genes duplicate and jump between species, shows how new functions arise.
learningObjectives: Calculate and interpret dN, dS and the ratio omega (dN/dS).
Explain codon-based likelihood tests for positive selection (site and branch models).
Describe the fates of duplicated genes: pseudogenisation, neofunctionalisation and subfunctionalisation.
Distinguish orthologs, paralogs, xenologs and in-paralogs and their implications for functional annotation.
Describe horizontal gene transfer mechanisms and evidence (atypical composition, phylogenetic incongruence).
Run a codeml or MEGA-based selection test on a small data set and report it with appropriate caution.

keyConcepts.definition: The number of non-synonymous (or synonymous) substitutions per non-synonymous (or synonymous) site.
Values below 1 indicate purifying selection, near 1 neutral evolution, and above 1 positive (diversifying) selection acting on amino acid changes.
A likelihood model allowing omega to vary among codons; M2a and M8 allow a class with omega over 1.
Comparing nested models by twice the difference in log-likelihood against a chi-squared distribution.
One duplicate acquires a new function while the other retains the old.
The ancestral functions are partitioned between duplicates by complementary degenerative mutations.
A doubling of the entire genome, an important source of raw genetic material in vertebrate and plant evolution.
Transfer of genetic material between organisms by means other than reproduction, by transformation, transduction or conjugation.
Fitting a gene tree inside a species tree to infer duplication, loss and transfer events.

deeper.beginner: Selection leaves a signature in the ratio of changes that alter the protein to those that do not. If non-synonymous changes are as common as silent ones, nothing is holding the protein back; if they are rarer, selection is protecting it; and if they are more common at some sites, something is pushing the protein to change. Duplication and horizontal transfer supply the raw material that selection can work on.
deeper.intermediate: Averaging omega over a whole gene hides signals because most sites are under purifying selection even in genes with a few adaptive sites. Site models in PAML codeml compare M1a (nearly neutral) with M2a (positive selection) and M7 (beta) with M8 (beta and omega) using likelihood ratio tests; Bayes empirical Bayes then identifies the candidate sites. Hands-on (about 3.5 h): align coding sequences as codons, build a tree, and run M1a vs M2a on a gene such as an immune or viral surface protein.
deeper.advanced: Tests of selection can give false positives when there is recombination, alignment errors or saturation of synonymous sites, so results should be checked with several methods (HyPhy: FEL, MEME, aBSREL). Gene duplication leads to dosage and redundancy effects; Lynch and Conery found that duplicate genes are lost or silenced at a high rate and that retained pairs often diverge in function. In bacteria, HGT shapes the pangenome and spreads antibiotic resistance genes through plasmids and integrative elements, which can be detected by unusual GC content, codon usage or phylogenetic conflict.

commonMistakes: Concluding positive selection from an average omega over an entire gene.
Applying dN/dS to closely related populations (within species), where polymorphism and deleterious variants distort the ratio.
Annotating a gene by its best BLAST hit without checking whether it is an ortholog or a paralog.

units.title: Protein Structure Prediction and Homology Modelling (Practical)
units.hook: For fifty years the 'protein folding problem' was a grand challenge: given a sequence, can you predict its three-dimensional structure? In 2020 AlphaFold2 came close enough to being a solution that it changed how structural biologists work. Yet the older idea of building a model from a related known structure is still taught because it explains why prediction works and when to be careful.
learningObjectives: Explain why sequence determines structure and why structure is more conserved than sequence.
Carry out template-based (homology) modelling: template search, alignment, model building, refinement and validation.
Interpret AlphaFold outputs, especially pLDDT and predicted aligned error (PAE).
Validate models using Ramachandran plots, clash scores (MolProbity) and QMEAN or similar scores.
Compare a homology model with an AlphaFold model and an experimental structure in a viewer.
State the limitations of predicted structures for drug design (conformational states, ligands, side chains).

keyConcepts.definition: An experimentally solved protein structure used as the basis for modelling a related sequence.
Building a 3D model of a target protein from its alignment to one or more templates; reliable when sequence identity is above about 30 percent.
A deep-learning system that predicts protein structure from sequence and multiple sequence alignment, with per-residue confidence estimates.
Predicted local distance difference test (0-100); above 90 very high confidence, 70-90 confident, 50-70 low and below 50 often disordered.
Predicted aligned error: expected position error in Angstroms of one residue when the structure is aligned on another; reveals confidence in domain arrangement.
A plot of backbone phi and psi angles showing which combinations are sterically allowed.
Checking stereochemistry, packing, clashes and statistical potential to judge model quality.
The archive of experimentally determined macromolecular structures (X-ray, NMR, cryo-EM).
A protein segment lacking a stable fold, which predictors tend to give low confidence.

deeper.beginner: If you know the structure of a protein, you have a very good idea of what its cousin looks like, because structure changes more slowly than sequence. Homology modelling aligns your sequence to the known structure and rebuilds the differences. AlphaFold learned the patterns from hundreds of thousands of known structures and millions of sequences, and can often predict the fold without a close template.
deeper.intermediate: In SWISS-MODEL the workflow is: paste the sequence, search templates by BLAST and HHblits against the SWISS-MODEL template library, choose by coverage, sequence identity and GMQE, build the model, and check QMEAN. Models from templates with over 50 percent identity usually have backbone errors of about 1-2 Angstroms in conserved regions, while loops and side chains are less accurate. Hands-on (about 4 h): build a homology model of a protein of interest, retrieve the AlphaFold model from the AlphaFold Database, superimpose them in ChimeraX or PyMOL, colour by pLDDT, and run MolProbity.
deeper.advanced: AlphaFold2 predicts one confident conformation, which may be neither the apo nor the ligand-bound state, and it does not place ligands, cofactors or ions (newer systems extend to complexes and ligands). High pLDDT does not guarantee the correct relative orientation of domains, which PAE addresses. For docking, predicted structures can work well when binding site side chains are accurate but may need refinement, induced fit or molecular dynamics. Alternatives and complements include RoseTTAFold, ESMFold (language-model based and fast), and Foldseek for structure-based searching.

commonMistakes: Treating high-confidence regions as proof of function; confidence is about the fold, not biology.
Using a model without validating it or checking that the template covers the region of interest.
Assuming AlphaFold structures show ligand-bound or physiologically specific conformations.

units.title: Molecular Dynamics Simulation (Practical)
units.hook: A crystal structure is a snapshot. Real proteins breathe, flex and sometimes open a hidden pocket for a fleeting moment. Molecular dynamics is a computational microscope that applies Newton's laws to every atom and shows the movie that the snapshot could only suggest.
learningObjectives: Explain the basic MD algorithm: forces from a force field, integration of equations of motion, time step.
Describe force-field terms (bonded and non-bonded) and name commonly used force fields.
Explain periodic boundary conditions, long-range electrostatics (PME), thermostats and barostats.
Set up and run the GROMACS lysozyme-in-water workflow: topology, box, solvation, ions, minimisation, NVT, NPT and production.
Analyse a trajectory with RMSD, RMSF, radius of gyration and hydrogen bonds.
Discuss sampling limits and when enhanced sampling or free-energy methods are needed.

keyConcepts.definition: A set of functions and parameters describing the potential energy of a system as a function of atom positions (for example AMBER, CHARMM, OPLS, GROMOS).
Energy terms for bond stretching, angle bending and torsion (dihedral) rotation.
Lennard-Jones (van der Waals) and Coulomb electrostatic interactions between atoms not directly bonded.
The interval between successive force calculations, typically 2 fs when bonds to hydrogen are constrained.
The simulation box is replicated in space so a molecule leaving one side re-enters the opposite side, avoiding surface artefacts.
A method for accurate handling of long-range electrostatics in periodic systems.
Stages that bring the system to the target temperature (constant volume) and pressure (constant pressure) before the production run.
Root-mean-square deviation from a reference structure over time; root-mean-square fluctuation per residue.
Methods such as metadynamics, replica exchange or umbrella sampling to cross energy barriers that plain MD rarely crosses.

deeper.beginner: In MD the computer calculates the force on each atom from every other atom, moves them a tiny step, recalculates and repeats millions of times. The result is a trajectory showing how the protein moves in water at body temperature. Simulations are only as good as the force field and the time they run; many important events are slower than what can be simulated.
deeper.intermediate: A typical protein-in-water system has tens of thousands of atoms, mostly water. After energy minimisation to remove clashes, NVT equilibration (about 100 ps) stabilises temperature and NPT equilibration stabilises pressure and density, then production runs of tens to hundreds of nanoseconds follow. Hands-on (about 4 h): follow the GROMACS lysozyme tutorial, then plot potential energy, temperature, pressure, RMSD of the backbone and RMSF per residue, and examine the structure in a viewer. A flat RMSD plateau suggests equilibrium on that timescale, not proof of convergence.
deeper.advanced: Accuracy depends on the force field and water model (TIP3P, TIP4P-Ew); intrinsically disordered proteins and charged groups can be poorly represented in some combinations. Ligands need compatible parameters (GAFF, CGenFF), generated and checked carefully. Binding free energies can be estimated with MM-PBSA (cheap, approximate) or alchemical methods (FEP, TI), which are more rigorous but expensive. GPU acceleration has brought microsecond simulations within reach of single workstations.

commonMistakes: Treating a single short trajectory as proof of stability or a binding mode; use replicates and longer runs.
Skipping equilibration or ignoring warnings during grompp.
Interpreting RMSD alone; per-residue fluctuations and structural features matter too.

units.title: The Drug Discovery Pipeline and Target Selection
units.hook: Imatinib, the pill that turned a fatal leukaemia into a manageable condition for many patients, began as a protein-kinase inhibitor idea and ended as a landmark of rational design. Behind every approved drug are years of target choices, failed compounds and carefully designed experiments, and computers now help at nearly every stage.
learningObjectives: Outline the stages from target identification to approval and the typical time, cost and attrition.
Describe how targets are identified and validated (genetics, omics, knock-down, CRISPR).
Explain hit finding strategies: HTS, fragment-based, virtual screening, natural products.
Distinguish hit, lead and candidate and the properties optimised in lead optimisation.
Compare structure-based and ligand-based drug design and when each is used.
Navigate PDB, UniProt, ChEMBL and PubChem to collect target and ligand information.

keyConcepts.definition: A biomolecule (usually a protein) whose modulation is expected to give a therapeutic benefit.
Evidence that modulating the target changes disease-relevant biology, from genetics, cell models and animal models.
Automated testing of hundreds of thousands of compounds in a biochemical or cellular assay to find hits.
Screening small low-affinity fragments and growing or linking them into potent leads guided by structure.
Optimising confirmed hits for potency, selectivity and drug-like properties.
Using the 3D structure of the target (and docking) to design or select ligands.
Using known active compounds, for example pharmacophores and QSAR, when the target structure is unknown.
The loss of candidates during development, mostly in clinical trials due to lack of efficacy or toxicity.
The property of a drug acting on multiple targets, which may be beneficial or cause side effects.

deeper.beginner: Developing a drug resembles solving a puzzle with many pieces that must fit at once: the molecule must bind its target tightly, avoid other targets, reach the right tissue, survive the body's metabolism and not harm the patient. Early computational filters save time and money by discarding hopeless candidates before anyone makes them in a lab.
deeper.intermediate: From target identification to market approval typically takes 10-15 years and well over a billion US dollars when failures are included, and most candidates entering clinical trials fail. Human genetic evidence (for example loss-of-function variants that protect against disease) increases the chance that a target will succeed. Computational methods fall into structure-based (docking, MD, FEP) and ligand-based (similarity, pharmacophore, QSAR) approaches, and large public databases (ChEMBL, PubChem, PDB) supply the data. Natural-product libraries from local biodiversity offer chemical diversity but need careful dereplication and ADMET evaluation.
deeper.advanced: Targets are often classified by druggability, with GPCRs, kinases, ion channels, nuclear receptors and proteases historically the most tractable; protein-protein interactions and transcription factors have been harder to drug but new modalities (PROTACs, molecular glues, covalent inhibitors, antibodies) are expanding what is druggable. Phenotypic screening rediscovered many first-in-class drugs, so target-based and phenotypic strategies are complementary. Network pharmacology argues that effective drugs often act on several nodes of a disease network, and computational polypharmacology tries to predict these profiles.

commonMistakes: Believing computers can replace experiments; they prioritise compounds, which still have to be made and tested.
Assuming a tight binder is a good drug without considering ADMET and selectivity.
Confusing a target with a drug, or in vitro potency with clinical efficacy.

units.title: Molecular Docking and Virtual Screening (Practical)
units.hook: Docking asks a deceptively simple question: if I place this small molecule into that pocket, how would it sit, and how snugly? Run a million times against a compound library it becomes virtual screening, a way to cherry-pick a few dozen candidates for the lab from a vast chemical space.
learningObjectives: Explain the two components of docking: conformational search and scoring.
Prepare a receptor and ligands properly (remove waters selectively, add hydrogens, assign charges, protonation, tautomers).
Define a search box around a binding site and run AutoDock Vina.
Validate a docking protocol by redocking a co-crystallised ligand and computing RMSD.
Evaluate virtual screening with decoys, enrichment factor and ROC curves.
Interpret docking poses by visualising hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic and pi interactions and be aware of scoring limitations.

keyConcepts.definition: Predicting the binding pose and estimating the affinity of a ligand within a receptor site.
A function estimating binding free energy from the pose; force-field based, empirical, knowledge-based or machine-learned.
The region of the receptor in which the ligand is allowed to move during docking.
Docking the co-crystallised ligand back into its own structure; success is typically an RMSD under 2 Angstroms.
Treating the receptor as fixed (common) or allowing selected side chains or backbone to move.
Ranking large compound libraries by predicted binding to prioritise compounds for testing.
How many more actives are found in the top fraction of a ranked list than would be expected by chance.
The file format used by AutoDock Vina holding coordinates, partial charges and atom types, plus torsion information for ligands.
Property-matched compounds presumed inactive, used to test whether a docking method can separate actives from inactives.

deeper.beginner: Think of the receptor pocket as a lock and the ligand as a key that can wiggle. The search algorithm tries many orientations and bends; the scoring function guesses how good each fit is. Scores help you rank, but the fits are only as reliable as the structure and the scoring function. Analogy break: real binding also depends on water, protein flexibility and entropy, which most scoring functions treat crudely.
deeper.intermediate: Preparation matters more than the program. Retain structurally important waters, choose protonation states for His, Asp, Glu at pH 7.4, and generate 3D ligand conformers with RDKit or Open Babel; convert to PDBQT with ADFR tools or Meeko. Hands-on (about 4.5 h): choose a PDB entry with a ligand, redock it with Vina and report RMSD, dock a small set of known actives and decoys, rank by score, and visualise the top pose. Vina scores are in kcal/mol, but the numbers only roughly correlate with experimental affinity, so use them for ranking, not for absolute predictions.
deeper.advanced: Scoring functions are tuned to reproduce poses and rank ligands but are poor at predicting absolute affinities, especially for charged or metal-binding ligands. Ultra-large library docking (Lyu et al. 2019) screened hundreds of millions of virtual molecules and found potent new chemotypes, showing how scale increases hit rates but also the number of false positives. Rescoring with MM-GBSA, MD simulations or free-energy calculations improves ranking for a short list. Always compare against appropriate controls, inspect poses for plausible interactions, and confirm hits experimentally.

commonMistakes: Taking a Vina score as a measured binding energy.
Skipping validation: always redock a known ligand and test enrichment before screening.
Docking with an unprepared structure (wrong protonation, missing atoms, a bound ligand left in place).

units.title: Ligand-Based Design, QSAR, Pharmacophores and ADMET (Practical)
units.hook: Sometimes you do not have the structure of the target, only a handful of molecules that work and many that do not. The ligand-based toolkit learns what the actives have in common, predicts new ones and checks whether they can survive the journey through a human body.
learningObjectives: Calculate molecular descriptors and fingerprints and use Tanimoto similarity.
Build and validate a simple QSAR model and describe its applicability domain.
Develop a pharmacophore hypothesis from actives and use it to screen compounds.
Apply Lipinski's rule of five, Veber rules and PAINS filters and know their limits.
Predict ADMET properties with SwissADME and interpret results critically.
Write a short RDKit script that reads SMILES, computes properties and applies filters.

keyConcepts.definition: A text notation for molecular structures that can be parsed by software such as RDKit.
A numerical property calculated from structure, such as molecular weight, logP, topological polar surface area or hydrogen-bond donors.
A bit-string encoding of structural features, such as Morgan (ECFP) circular fingerprints; used for similarity searching.
A similarity measure between two fingerprints: shared bits divided by the union of bits.
Quantitative structure-activity relationship: a model relating descriptors to biological activity.
The chemical space in which a QSAR model's predictions are reliable.
The 3D arrangement of features (donor, acceptor, hydrophobic, aromatic, charged) required for activity.
Lipinski's guideline for oral bioavailability: molecular weight up to 500, logP up to 5, no more than 5 H-bond donors and 10 acceptors.
Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity: properties that determine whether an active molecule becomes a usable drug.

deeper.beginner: Ligand-based design is a pattern-finding game. If every active compound shares a hydrogen-bond donor three Angstroms from an aromatic ring, then a new molecule with the same arrangement is a good candidate. ADMET filters then ask whether the molecule can be absorbed, avoid being destroyed or toxic and reach where it is needed.
deeper.intermediate: A QSAR model is only as good as its data: a few dozen consistent assay results from a single series can support a local model, but predicting across diverse chemotypes needs thousands of compounds. Validate with cross-validation and an external test set that the model has never seen, and report both R2 and Q2 or RMSE. Hands-on (about 4 h): in RDKit, load SMILES for known inhibitors of a target from ChEMBL, compute Lipinski descriptors and Morgan fingerprints, cluster by Tanimoto similarity, train a random-forest regressor on pIC50, and test on a held-out set; then run SwissADME on the top compounds and compare predictions.
deeper.advanced: Lipinski's rules were derived from orally administered drugs in clinical development in the 1990s and do not apply well to natural products, peptides, antibiotics or modern modalities (so-called beyond-rule-of-five space). QSAR faces activity cliffs, where small structural changes cause large activity changes, violating the similar-property principle, and random splits overestimate performance, so scaffold or time splits are better. The OECD principles for QSAR validation (defined endpoint, unambiguous algorithm, applicability domain, appropriate validation, mechanistic interpretation) are a useful checklist.

commonMistakes: Believing a molecule that passes Lipinski's rules is a drug; the rules only filter for likely oral absorption.
Evaluating a QSAR model on its training data or on a random split of near-duplicate compounds.
Trusting predicted ADMET values as measured properties.

units.title: Machine Learning in Drug Design and Integrated Mini-Project (Practical)
units.hook: In 2020 a neural network trained on a few thousand molecules flagged halicin, a compound that had been sitting in a library, as a potent antibiotic with a novel structure, and experiments confirmed it. Machine learning is now woven into every stage of computational drug design, and the best results come from people who know exactly what could go wrong.
learningObjectives: Explain how graph neural networks and fingerprint-based models represent molecules.
Describe generative models for molecules and what they can and cannot guarantee.
Identify common failure modes: data leakage, biased training sets, activity cliffs and over-optimistic validation.
Describe how AI-predicted structures and models fit into the structure-based pipeline.
Plan and run an integrated mini-project: choose a target, retrieve or model its structure, dock and rank compounds, filter by ADMET and write a short report.
Present results with appropriate uncertainty and propose experimental validation.

keyConcepts.definition: A neural network that learns directly from the molecular graph (atoms as nodes, bonds as edges).
A model that proposes new molecules, for example by sampling from a learned chemical space or by optimising a property.
When information from the test set leaks into training, giving unrealistic performance estimates.
Splitting data so that test molecules have different core scaffolds from the training molecules, a stricter test of generalisation.
A pair of similar compounds with very different activity, which challenges similarity-based models.
Methods that show which features drive a prediction, helping chemists decide whether it is plausible.
An iterative process in which a model selects the most informative compounds to test next.
Documented, version-controlled steps with fixed random seeds and recorded software versions so others can repeat the analysis.
The region of chemical space where a trained model's predictions can be trusted.

deeper.beginner: A machine-learning model is a very flexible curve-fitter. If you feed it good, diverse, well-measured data it learns real structure-activity patterns; if you feed it a biased or leaky data set, it will confidently learn the wrong thing. The ability to tell the two situations apart is the key skill of computational drug design in the AI era.
deeper.intermediate: In practice the pipeline is: collect data (ChEMBL), curate it (standardise structures, remove duplicates, check assay comparability), choose a representation (fingerprints, descriptors or graphs), train with proper splits and report uncertainty. Mini-project (about 3 h of practical time plus self-study): choose a well-characterised target with a PDB structure and known actives, validate docking by redocking, screen 50-100 compounds including known actives and decoys, apply drug-likeness filters, and write a one-page report that states what is predicted, what is validated and what would need testing.
deeper.advanced: Models trained on public data inherit their biases, such as an over-representation of well-studied targets and chemotypes, and ChEMBL assay data come from different labs with different protocols. Generative models often propose molecules that are hard to synthesise, so synthesisability scores and retrosynthesis tools are used alongside property optimisation. Prospective validation (testing predictions for compounds not yet made) is far more convincing than retrospective benchmarking, and the halicin and ultra-large docking papers are good examples of the former. The best workflows combine physics-based (docking, MD) and data-driven methods.

commonMistakes: Reporting performance on a random split of a data set with near-duplicate compounds.
Accepting a model's confident prediction without examining its training data or applicability domain.
Treating AI-generated molecules as ready-to-use: synthesisability, toxicity and novelty all need checking.
